edges.description: The primary enzymatic lesion is loss of muscle-type phosphofructokinase activity.
Loss of PFKM function blocks the phosphofructokinase step in skeletal-muscle glycolysis.
PFKM deficiency reduces erythrocyte glycolytic phosphofructokinase function.
Impaired skeletal-muscle glycolysis limits exertional energy production.
Exertional glycolytic energy failure contributes to muscle cramping.
Inability to use glucose as a muscle energy source is associated with exertional myalgia.
Exertional muscle injury can lead to myoglobinuria.
Severe exertional muscle injury can manifest as rhabdomyolysis.
The PFKM block may reroute glucose-6-phosphate through the pentose phosphate pathway during exertion, with downstream nucleotide and amino-acid metabolism contributing to abnormal ammonia generation.
intermediate_mechanisms: pentose phosphate pathway entry downstream of the PFKM block

nodes.description: Unlike in glycogenolytic defects such as McArdle disease (GSD V), consuming carbohydrates immediately before exercise exacerbates exercise intolerance in GSD VII. Because PFKM deficiency blocks utilization of both blood glucose and muscle glycogen, a pre-exercise carbohydrate load cannot supply pyruvate while the resulting insulin surge suppresses peripheral and intramyocellular lipolysis, depriving skeletal muscle of alternative oxidative free fatty acid substrates ("out-of-wind" phenomenon).

evidence.reference_title: Polyglucosan storage myopathies.
evidence.snippet: These diseases frequently involve both skeletal and cardiac muscle tissue, causing myopathy with muscle weakness and wasting, and cardiomyopathy with arrhythmia, conduction block, and cardiac failure. Mutations in eight human genes are known to be associated with polyglucosan storage involving muscle, namely GYG1, GBE1, RBCK1 (HOIL-1), PFKM, EPM2A, EPM2B (NHLRC1), PRDM8, and PRKAG2.
